title: Ingress/Egress + mTLS Routing Playbook (multi-region)
content:
Purpose:
Provide a pragmatic, checklist-style playbook for network path and routing decisions across multi-region Redwood environments. Focus is on ingress/egress placement, mTLS trust boundaries, service-mesh tradeoffs, and control-plane responsibilities for routing policies and failover.

Audience:
Platform engineers, infra SREs, and architects who own cluster/network topology, and engineers implementing routing policies for Hosted/Dedicated/Private deployments.

Goals / non-goals:
- Goals:
  - Minimize blast radius while keeping predictable latency for inference traffic.
  - Provide clear mTLS trust model and cert lifecycle for both north-south and east-west traffic.
  - Standardize routing policy primitives (priority, locality, fallback) across control plane and data plane.
  - Offer actionable patterns for multi-region failover and cross-region routing.
- Non-goals:
  - Prescribing a single mesh implementation; rather, score tradeoffs and recommended defaults.

Assumptions & constraints:
- Customer traffic enters via public endpoints (hosted) or via VPC peering / Direct Connect (private).
- Inference runtime pods are latency-sensitive; unnecessary proxy hops increase tail latency.
- Cryptographic keys for certs need to integrate with KMS/HSM (private deployments may use customer KMS).
- We operate multiple regions with regional control plane replicas and a central policy plane for global configuration.

High-level topology options (with guidance):
1) Ingress Gateway per region + regional mesh for east-west
   - Data plane: edge LB (NLB/ILB) -> regional ingress gateway (Envoy) -> regional mesh sidecars -> svc
   - Control plane: regional control-plane replica for routing decisions, global policy store for config propagation
   - Pros: Local failover, regional autonomy, lower cross-region egress cost when requests stay local
   - Cons: Extra hop (gateway), sidecar overhead, certificate surface bigger
   - When to use: Hosted/Dedicated where multi-tenant and fine-grained L7 routing required

2) Terminate TLS at edge + short-circuit to pod (meshless east-west)
   - Data plane: edge LB -> ingress (terminates TLS, performs auth) -> direct to pod (no sidecar)
   - Pros: Lower CPU/memory per pod, fewer hops -> lower p50/p95
   - Cons: Harder to enforce uniform mTLS between services, more responsibility on ingress to implement authz
   - When to use: High-throughput inference paths where per-pod sidecar overhead is unacceptable and where we accept centralized L7 enforcement

3) Sidecar-first (full mesh) 
   - Data plane: LB -> ingress gateway -> sidecar-to-sidecar mTLS throughout cluster
   - Pros: Consistent security model, easy telemetry, policy enforcement
   - Cons: Increased tail latency, resource overhead, complex cross-region settings
   - When to use: Private deployments that prioritize zero-trust and telemetry over absolute tail latency

Recommended default for Redwood (opinionated): hybrid pattern
- In hosted & dedicated: use regional ingress gateways + selective sidecar injection for control-plane and inter-service paths that need auth/observability; allow sidecarless hot-paths for runtime inference pods (opt-in).
- In private/on-prem: favor full sidecar mesh if customer requires strict zero-trust and has capacity for sidecars.

mTLS trust model and certificate lifecycle:
- Root of trust:
  - Hosted: we operate our CA (private PKI), keys stored in cloud KMS with regular rotation (90d).
  - Dedicated: Redwood-managed CA, but keys stored and rotated in customer-controlled KMS if requested (contract).
  - Private: customer-managed CA, we support SPIRE/ACME integration and offline signing for air-gapped installs.
- mTLS tiers:
  - North-South (client -> edge): TLS terminated at ingress gateway. Strong client auth for customer-managed endpoints (mutual TLS for private endpoints). Use JWT verification at gateway for hosted API.
  - East-West (svc -> svc): prefer mTLS between proxies (sidecars) or use a lightweight in-kernel approach for sidecarless mTLS (see eBPF note below) for hot-paths.
- Cert distribution:
  - Use cert-manager or SPIRE agents for per-node/per-pod cert issuance with short-lived certs (1h - 24h depending on threat model).
  - Fallback: long-lived node certs for control-plane components with constrained rotation windows and documented rollover playbooks.
- Rotation & revocation:
  - CRL is hard at scale; prefer short lived certs + central revocation by issuing deny-list at ingress gateways + CRL for control-plane admin components.

Service mesh considerations (Envoy + Istio / Linkerd alternatives):
- Observability vs latency tradeoff: Envoy gives powerful L7 features but has non-trivial CPU. Linkerd is lighter but less feature-rich. If inference runtime pods are resource-constrained, prefer meshless hot-paths with gateway-level L7.
- Sidecar lifecycle ops: need robust rollout (gradual injection), canaries for sidecar versions, and automatic cleanup for terminated pods to avoid cert leakage.
- Network policies and pod security: ensure egress to KMS/CA endpoints is whitelisted. For private installs, document allowed IPs for CA endpoints.
- Policy consistency: use a central policy repo (gitops) that gets propagated to regional control-plane replicas; policies should be expressed in a small set of primitives: match (path/host/headers), priority, locality_preference, failover_targets, transform_rules. Keep these small to avoid explosion of rules.

Routing policies primitives (recommended):
- match: host/path/header
- weight: split percentage for canaries/A-B
- locality_preference: prefer local region, then sibling region list
- fallback_policy: immediate, degraded (lower QPS), or queue
- latency_sla_ms: if path exceeds threshold, trigger fallback to lower-cost model variant or smaller model
- circuit_breaker: max concurrency / timeout

Multi-region failover patterns:
- Active-active with locality aware routing (preferred):
  - Use DNS geo + LB affinity to keep traffic regional. If regional capacity insufficient, promote next-best region per routing policy.
- Active-passive for cold standby:
  - Keep warm instances behind regional ingress but only route on failure detection (health and capacity signals).
- Cross-region considerations:
  - Keep KV caches local, avoid cross-region KV reads in hot path. Use async replication or tiered cache eviction policies.
  - Define SLOs for inter-region latency and only permit cross-region routing when latency budget allows (compare measured RTT + service processing).

Control plane design for routing policies:
- Components:
  - Global policy store (gitops repo + central DB) - authoritative desired state.
  - Region control-plane replicas: subscribe to global store, manage local config, do local leader election for region-specific decisions.
  - Local decision engine: evaluates runtime telemetry and can alter routing for emergency (circuit-breaker, scale-to-zero, failover).
- Safety limits:
  - Changes from global policy must go through staged rollout: staging -> canary region -> full.
  - Emergency rollback: always expose a single global kill-switch at the policy level to revert to simple round-robin regional fallback.

Health checks, telemetry, and signals to drive routing:
- Health = Liveness + Readiness + custom inference health (model loaded, cache warm). Use a 3-state readiness so control plane can detect degraded vs down.
- Capacity signals: CPU/GPU utilization, queue depth, p50/p95 latency, model-quality degradation alerts. Metrics aggregated per model-version and per-region.
- Use these signals to automatically adjust weights or to trigger fallback policy. Keep ML-specific thresholds configurable per-model.

Edge cases and gotchas:
- mTLS termination at external gateways can expose backend nodes to plain HTTP; ensure gateway-to-backend is still encrypted or on private network.
- Cross-region TLS: ensure SNI preservation when proxying so routing decisions downstream can use host header.
- DDoS protection: edge LB + WAF in front; ensure cost-limited fallback policies to avoid expensive model serving during attack.
- Route flapping: add hysteresis to automatic failover to avoid thrash (cooldown windows).

Operational runbook (short checklist):
- Pre-deploy checks:
  - Policy linting passes (gitops).
  - Cert-manager/SPIRE agents healthy in every region.
  - Ingress gateway health and TLS chain validated.
- Rollout steps for new routing rule:
  - Add rule in gitops repo -> CI checks -> apply to staging region.
  - Observe for 30m, validate (latency, error rate, cost impact).
  - Canary to 1 additional region for 1h -> if stable roll to remaining regions.
- Incident: regional overload
  - Step 1: Trigger local autoscale and increase ingress weight cap temporarily.
  - Step 2: If capacity insufficient, promote fallback targets in policy (regional->sibling region).
  - Step 3: If cross-region traffic spikes cost or latency, reroute to lower-cost model variants (per-model fallback).

Migration and incremental adoption plan:
- Start by deploying regional ingress gateways and implementing north-south auth at the gateway.
- Adopt sidecar for control-plane and admin services first (observability + policy enforcement).
- Introduce sidecarless hot-paths: benchmark end-to-end tail latency and determine which models should be hot-path.
- Roll out cert short-lifetimes and automated rotation.

Open questions / TODOs (notes to follow up):
- Decide default cert lifetime for inference pods (1h vs 24h) — tradeoff between security and signing load.
- Evaluate eBPF-based mTLS (Cilium) for sidecarless strong identity with less CPU overhead. Prototype on small fleet.
- Capacity-aware routing: implement cost-aware scoring model to prefer cheaper variants under load.
- Define SDK-level client retry/backoff primitives to play nicely with local failover and avoid thundering herd.

References and prior art:
- Envoy docs: TLS origins and SNI routing
- SPIRE for workload identity + certs
- Cilium eBPF for sidecarless policies
- GitHub PR: platform/pull/412 (ingress gateway rollout)

Appendix: minimal example policy (human-readable)
- match: host: inference.redwood.ai; path: /v1/generate
- weight: 80 -> region-us-west, 20 -> region-eu-west
- locality_preference: [us-west, us-east, eu-west]
- fallback_policy: promote next region after 3 consecutive 5xx OR cpu_util > 85% for 2 minutes
- latency_sla_ms: 300

Notes to self:
- Keep the playbook lightweight; teams want decision trees not encyclopedias.
- Surface cost impact with every recommendation (per-token cost bump if adding extra hop).
